Every face and every body
4. One Picture, Three Moments

Human examples are limited, and Allah's is the highest example (Qur'an 16:60), but a picture can still help the heart. Think of a craftsman. First he studies the measure and designs the work; that is the idea behind **Al-Khaliq**. Then the work comes into being as a separate thing; that is **Al-Bari'**. Then comes the detail: the lines of the face, the colour, the finish; that is **Al-Musawwir**. And Allah is beyond any comparison. He needs no tools, no material and no time.

The Qur'an itself walks through these stages in the womb: *"Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot, and We made the clot into a lump, and We made from the lump bones, and We covered the bones with flesh; then We developed him into another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators."* (Qur'an 23:14). And then: *"It is He who forms you in the wombs however He wills"* (3:6). The womb again, the same رَحِم that carries the Names Ar-Rahman and Ar-Raheem. The place where mercy and creation meet.
5. Essence Together
Al-Khaliq plans it, Al-Bari' brings it forth, Al-Musawwir shapes it. Nothing exists, and no face is the face it is, except by Him.
6. For You, the Servant

**Before you were anything.** There was a plan for you before you were a thought in anyone's mind. **While you were nothing.** You were brought out of nothing, distinct and complete. **When you took form.** You were shaped in a place no one could see, in a face that no one chose. Three Names, and you stand at the end of all of them. So the question is not whether you have a reason to be grateful; it is how long you will wait before you start.
The Ever-Forgiving, Again & Again
to cover and to shield, so that the thing covered is protected from harm.

Ibn Faris says that the root of this word is the idea of covering. The helmet a warrior wears is called **مِغْفَر**, because it covers and protects his head. So forgiveness in Arabic is not only "letting it go." It is covering the sin and protecting the person from its consequence.
The Qur'an uses three forms from this one root, and each adds something:
Name
What it shows
He forgives: the act itself (Qur'an 40:3)
He forgives abundantly, with great depth of forgiveness
He forgives again and again, without ever tiring of forgiving
الْغَفَّارُ: The One who forgives sins over and over, covers them, and protects His servant from their consequence.
مَغْفِرَة (forgiveness) · غُفْرَان (pardon) · اسْتِغْفَار (asking forgiveness) · مِغْفَر (helmet)

This is Nuh speaking to his people after nine hundred and fifty years of calling them. After all that time, his advice is still the same: ask forgiveness. And he gives them the reason in a single Name: **غَفَّارًا**. He is always ready to forgive.

Notice the four things attached to this forgiveness: he repented, believed, did good, and stayed on the guidance. The door is open, but it is a door for someone who actually walks through it. Allah's mercy toward the one who returns is vast, and He calls that very person to keep going.
And remember the ayah from Ar-Raheem, Qur'an 39:53: *"Do not despair of the mercy of Allah."* The Name Al-Ghaffar is the reason that despair has no place in the believer.

In a hadith qudsi, Allah says: "O son of Adam, as long as you call upon Me and hope in Me, I forgive you for what you have done, and I do not mind. O son of Adam, if you came to Me with an earth-full of sins and then met Me without associating anything with Me, I would meet you with an earth-full of forgiveness."
Al-Ghaffar is the One who forgives again and again, who covers the sins of His servants and protects them from their consequences, however often they return.

The shaytan has two lines. Before the sin, he says: it is small, do it. After the sin, he says: it is too big, give up. Al-Ghaffar answers the second line. Your sin is not bigger than His forgiveness, and your return is not a nuisance to Him. The word is built on repetition, so that you never think you have used up your chances.

The Prophet ﷺ, whose sins were forgiven, said that he asked Allah's forgiveness more than seventy times in a day (Sahih al-Bukhari 6307). If he did, what excuse is left for us? Istighfar is not only for the one who just sinned. It is a way of living in front of Al-Ghaffar.
When did you last return to Him, and did you go as if He would refuse you or as if He had been waiting?
The Subduer, Who Overcomes All
to overcome and subdue completely, from a position of height.
The intensive pattern again: not only does He overcome, He overcomes everything, continuously.
Compare it with its close neighbour in the Qur'an, **الْقَاهِر** (6:18), which names the act, while Al-Qahhar says that this overcoming is unceasing and complete.
The Name Al-Jabbar spoke of power that mends and restores. Al-Qahhar speaks of power that no creature can stand against.
الْقَهَّارُ: The One who subdues everything beneath His power, and whom nothing can overcome.
قَاهِر (the Overcomer) · قَهْر (overpowering) · مَقْهُور (one who is overcome) · قُهِرَ (was subdued)

Yusuf, in prison, asks his two fellow prisoners a question: are many scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer? Look at who is speaking and where. He is in a cell, with no power at all, and he is the one who states most clearly who actually holds all of it. When the cell is dark, the Name Al-Qahhar is the one that tells you who is really in control.
"To whom belongs the dominion this Day? To Allah, the One, the Prevailing."
On the Day of Judgement this question is asked and there is no one to answer except Him. Every power that people feared will be gone. All that remains is the One and the Subduer.
The Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Resurrection Allah will take hold of the earth and fold up the heavens in His right hand, and then say: "I am the King. Where are the kings of the earth?"
Al-Qahhar is the One who subdues all creation, to whom everything is subject, and who cannot be overcome by anything.

For the oppressor, this is a Name of warning: your power is borrowed, and the One who lent it can take it back. For the oppressed, it is a Name of comfort: no tyrant who ever lived escaped it. Pharaoh's army, the greatest power of his age, was drowned in water. The same Name is working today.

And it is also a Name for you in a more personal way. There are things in your own life that feel unbeatable: a habit, a fear, a situation. They are all creatures, and every creature is under the Subduer. You do not have to fight them by your own strength. Ask Al-Qahhar for help against what overpowers you.
What in your life feels too strong for you, and have you asked the One who overcomes all things to overcome it?
The Bestower of Gifts Without Measure
a gift given freely, without expecting anything in return.

A هِبَة in Arabic is a pure gift. It is not a payment, a loan or a trade. The giver does not need anything back, and the receiver has not earned it. That is the exact meaning at the base of this Name.
As with the Names before it, the pattern shows intensity and constancy: He gives again and again.
So Al-Wahhab does not give once. He gives continually, without any need, without being asked, and without His treasury ever running low.
Every gift in your life, your life itself, was a هِبَة, not a wage.
الْوَهَّابُ: The One who continually gives freely, with no need and no return, far beyond what anyone deserves.
هِبَة (gift) · مَوْهِبَة (talent, a given ability) · وَاهِب (giver) · اتِّهَاب (receiving a gift)

This is how the people of understanding pray: they do not ask for a reward; they ask for a gift. **وَهَبْ لَنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةً**. Even their request is for mercy that comes from Him, because no deed can pay for what they need. And they ask it right after asking Him to keep their hearts firm, because the most precious gift is guidance that stays.

Zakariyya was old and his wife was barren, and he asked for a child. He did not ask as someone who deserved one; he asked as someone who knows Al-Wahhab. And he was answered. Whatever the situation looks like, the Name is the answer.
Even Sulayman, who was given a kingdom unlike any other, called the whole kingdom a gift, with the very Name Al-Wahhab.
The Prophet ﷺ said: "The right hand of Allah is full. Spending does not diminish it. It pours out night and day."
Al-Wahhab is the One who gives and gives without end, freely and without need of any return, and whose giving never decreases.

Look at your life as gifts, and the gratitude changes. Your eyesight, your family, the child who was given after years, the ability to read this page: you did not buy any of it. When you think you earned something, the heart gets proud. When you remember it was a هِبَة, the heart gets humble and grateful.

And ask big. When you ask Al-Wahhab, you are not asking someone who is limited. The prayers of Zakariyya and Sulayman were not small ones, and they were not turned back. Ask Him for what looks impossible, and ask as a servant asking his generous Lord.
What have you been treating as something you earned, which was in fact only ever given to you?
The Constant Provider of All
a continuing allotment given to be benefited from and lived on.

In Arabic and in the Qur'an, **رِزْق** is much wider than money. Your health is rizq. Your time, your spouse, your knowledge, the people who love you, a righteous child, a word of guidance, the very breath in your chest: all of it is rizq, because all of it is given to you to live on and benefit from.
The pattern of constant and repeated action: He provides without pause, to every creature, at every moment.
He provides the one who thanks Him and the one who does not. This is the same worldly mercy that we met in Ar-Rahman.
And the greatest provision is not food, but guidance.
الرَّزَّاقُ: The One who continually provides every creature with everything it needs to live and benefit.
رِزْق (provision) · رَازِق (provider) · مَرْزُوق (one who is provided for) · ارْتِزَاق (seeking a livelihood)

Notice what the ayah pairs with Ar-Razzaq: **ذُو الْقُوَّةِ الْمَتِينُ**, the Possessor of Strength, the Firm. His provision is backed by power. It cannot be cut off by anyone, because no one is stronger than the One who provides.
"And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision..."
**إِلَّا عَلَى اللَّهِ رِزْقُهَا**; He has taken it upon Himself. Every ant, every bird, every fish in the deep. He knows where it lives and what it needs.
And the ayah includes you in it: **وَإِيَّاكُمْ**, "and you as well." Some animals cannot even carry their own food, and Allah provides them. How would He forget you?
The Prophet ﷺ said: "If you relied upon Allah as He should be relied upon, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out in the morning hungry, and return in the evening full."
Ar-Razzaq is the One who provides every living thing with all it needs, continually, from sources it never expected and could never have produced itself.

Notice what the hadith about the birds says. The bird goes out. It does not stay in the nest waiting. Tawakkul is not the absence of effort; it is effort without the belief that effort is the source. You go out in the morning, and you know it is Ar-Razzaq who fills you in the evening.

This Name is the end of two diseases: the panic that your provision will run out, and the greed that makes you take from what is haram to secure it. What is yours will reach you, and what is not will never be yours. So seek it cleanly, and let the One who provides be the source of your peace.
Are you working hard for your provision while trusting its source, or trusting your own work as the source?
The Opener & the Just Judge
opening what is closed; and by extension, deciding and granting victory.

This root has three families of meaning in the Qur'an. **Opening**: a door, a path, a closed matter. **Judging**: the one who opens the case and decides between two sides. **Victory**: because when the matter is decided in your favour, the way is opened. All three come together in the Name Al-Fattah.
He opens again and again, and opens everything: closed doors of provision, doors of understanding, doors of mercy, doors of ease.
He also opens what no one else can open: hearts that were shut, a hardship that had no way out.
And He judges with perfect knowledge, which is why the Qur'an so often pairs this Name with **الْعَلِيم**.
الْفَتَّاحُ: The One who opens every closed door, who decides between His servants with truth, and who grants victory.
فَتْح (opening; victory) · مِفْتَاح (key) · فَاتِحَة (an opening) · فَتَحَ (He opened)

This is the ayah of the open and the closed door. If He opens a door of mercy, nobody can close it. If He closes one, nobody can open it. The whole of life is made of doors, and only One hand has the key to all of them.

And here, **يَفْتَحُ بَيْنَنَا بِالْحَقِّ**, He opens the case between us in truth. Every injustice that was never corrected in this life, every hidden wrong, will be decided by the One who is Al-Fattah and Al-'Alim, so that the verdict is perfectly just and perfectly informed.
"Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of those who give decision."

This is the prayer of the Prophet Shu'ayb and those with him: **افْتَحْ بَيْنَنَا**. A small, faithful group in front of a powerful, hostile people, and they hand the whole matter to the best of those who open.
The Prophet ﷺ taught us to say upon entering the mosque: "O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy." And upon leaving: "O Allah, I ask You for Your bounty."
Al-Fattah is the One who opens every closed door, whose opening no one can shut, and who decides between His servants with perfect truth.

When a door closes in your life, a job, a proposal, a way out, you have two choices. You can push at that door until you are tired, or you can ask the One who owns every door. That does not mean you stop acting. It means you act with your hand on the handle and your eyes on Al-Fattah.

And remember that you are surrounded by doors you cannot see: the door of understanding a verse, the door of a heart softening, the door of forgiveness. The best du'a at the threshold of a mosque is the same one a person can pray at the threshold of every day.
Which door in your life have you been pushing against, and have you asked the One who owns the key?
The All-Knowing
knowledge, and a sign by which a thing is known.
As with Ar-Raheem and Al-'Aziz, this pattern conveys a quality that is established in its owner. His knowledge is not acquired; it is part of who He is.
The Qur'an uses three forms of this Name: **عَالِم** (the knower), **عَلِيم** (the All-Knowing), and **عَلَّام** (the One who knows in the most intensive way, as in **عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوبِ**, 5:109).
Human knowledge begins in ignorance and is gained from outside. His begins from nothing, and never ends.
الْعَلِيمُ: The One whose knowledge encompasses everything: the seen and unseen, the past, present and future, the hidden and the open.
عِلْم (knowledge) · عَالِم (knower, scholar) · عَلَّام (the One who knows in the fullest way) · عَلَامَة (a sign)
"And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but that He knows it."
Look at how small the detail is: a single leaf. And the ayah continues to a seed in the darkness of the earth, and everything wet or dry. No grain of knowledge is outside His book.
"But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not."

This ayah explains the benefit of this Name for the believer. When something painful happens, you are looking at one frame; Al-'Alim sees the whole film. What you hate may be a mercy in disguise. Your trust is not blind trust; it is trust in a perfect Knower.
A single question, and its answer is another two Names: Al-Latif and Al-Khabir, which you will meet in this book.
From the du'a of istikhara taught by the Prophet ﷺ: "For You have power and I have none; You know and I do not know; and You are the Knower of the unseen."
Al-'Alim is the One whose knowledge has no limit and no beginning: He knows all that was, all that is, and all that will be, the hidden and the open alike.

The istikhara du'a is the Name Al-'Alim put into words. You are not saying: choose what I want. You are saying: I cannot see the end; You can. That is not weakness. It is the most intelligent thing a person with limited sight can do.

And it frees you from the exhausting need to understand everything. Some questions will not be answered in this life: why this happened, why not that. Al-'Alim knows. You do not have to carry the whole weight of understanding; you only have to carry the weight of obeying and trusting.
What have you been trying to understand completely, when you could have left it with the One who does?
The Withholder, Who Constricts as He Wills
to grasp, to hold back, and to draw in.

**قَبَضَ** is to take hold of something in the hand and close the fist. It is used for holding back provision, for drawing in, for taking something. And it is also used for the taking of souls, when Allah takes what He has lent.

An important point about this Name: it is never a Name of cruelty. Allah constricts out of wisdom, for a purpose that He knows. Scholars also stress that this Name and the next, Al-Basit, belong together. You should not think of one without the other.
An active participle: He is the One who does this, constantly, according to His wisdom.
He constricts provision, health, or ease for some, for a time, and for reasons that serve them even if they cannot see it.
He does it with perfect justice and mercy; the constriction is as much a part of His wisdom as the expansion.
الْقَابِضُ: The One who holds back, draws in and constricts whatever He wills, in perfect wisdom and justice.
قَبْض (grasping) · مَقْبُوض (held, taken) · قَبِيضَة (a handful) · انْقِبَاض (contraction)

Both Names sit in a single clause: **يَقْبِضُ وَيَبْصُۜطُ**. And what comes right before it? A call to give: *"Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan?"* The one who holds and expands is asking you to give. If your provision were truly yours, you could not lend it to Him. You are lending Him what He first gave you.

This is how a person misreads this Name. When Al-Qabid constricts, he concludes that he has been rejected. The Qur'an answers with a single word in the next ayah: **كَلَّا**, "No!" Constriction is not insult. It is a test, and it is also a form of care.
The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah is the One who sets prices, the One who constricts, the One who expands, the Provider."
Al-Qabid is the One who holds back and constricts as He wills, in perfect wisdom, and who has the right to give and to withhold alike.

Constriction is among the hardest things to carry: a tight month, a closed door, a heart that feels shut. The believer's answer is not to assume he was abandoned. It is to see Al-Qabid at work, and to remember that the hand that holds back is the hand of Ar-Rahman and Al-Hakim.

And the next time you feel your own heart tighten, know that this too can be the Name: the heart is constricted and expanded by Him. Ask for relief, but do not conclude that constriction means distance. Often it is the very moment when someone turns back.
Where you have been constricted, have you read it as rejection, or as the hand of a wise Lord who is holding you?
The Expander, Who Gives Abundance
to spread out, to extend and to expand.
**بَسَطَ** is to spread something out wide, like a carpet, like an open hand. It is used for expanding provision, for stretching out mercy, for widening the heart. It is the exact opposite of qabd.
Remember, as with the last Name, that you should hold both together. The One who expands is the One who constricts, and both are done in full wisdom.
An active participle: He is the One who does the expanding, continually.
He expands provision, so that the one who had little is given plenty; He expands the heart, so that what was tight becomes spacious; He expands life, and knowledge and strength.
And the expansion is also a test. The one who is given much is being asked how he will use it.
الْبَاسِطُ: The One who extends and expands provision, mercy and ease to whomever He wills, according to His wisdom.
بَسْط (expanding) · بِسَاط (carpet) · بَسِيط (simple, spread) · انْبِسَاط (gladness, an open heart)

Look at what the ayah ends with: **خَبِيرًا بَصِيرًا**, "All-Aware, All-Seeing" of His servants. His expansion and His constriction are both done with perfect knowledge of every servant: what he can bear, what would corrupt him, what would draw him closer.
"Allah extends provision for whom He wills and restricts."

The very next words in the ayah: *"And they rejoice in the worldly life, but the worldly life, compared to the Hereafter, is nothing but [brief] enjoyment."* Expansion is a gift, but it is a small and temporary one. Do not mistake it for the destination.
The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever loves to have his provision expanded and his life extended, let him keep his family ties."

Notice the word used for "expanded": **يُبْسَطَ**, from this very Name. And notice the cause: **رَحِمَهُ**, the same word رَحِم, the womb and kinship, from Ar-Rahman and Ar-Raheem. Whoever protects the ties of mercy is met by Al-Basit.
Al-Basit is the One who extends provision, mercy and ease to His servants as He wills, who opens hands and hearts, and whose expansion has no limit but His wisdom.

When Al-Basit expands you, the right response is to expand others. A heart that has been given room should make room: for the poor, for the relative who is difficult, for the person who made a mistake. The best way to thank the One who expands is to become, in your small way, a source of expansion for others.

And if you are ever in a time of ease, remember that it came from Him and can be taken by Him. Not with fear, but with gratitude. The believer is steady in both: grateful in the expanse, patient in the constriction.
When you were given room, did you use it to make room for others?
The Abaser, Who Lowers the Arrogant
to lower, to put down, to bring low.

**خَفَضَ** is to lower something: a voice, a wing, a rank. The scholars stress that this Name, like Ar-Rafi', is only fully understood when read with its pair. He lowers whom He lowers in justice, and the lowering is a response to something: arrogance, oppression, rebellion.
An active participle: He is the One who does this, as and when His wisdom decides.
Allah lowers the proud who refuse the truth, the tyrants who exalted themselves above their Lord, and those who looked down on others.

The Qur'an uses the same root for the best kind of lowering a servant can do: **وَاخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ**, "lower to your parents the wing of humility out of mercy" (17:24). The one who lowers himself for Allah is not the one He lowers.
الْخَافِضُ: The One who brings low whoever He wills, in justice, including those who raised themselves above the truth.
خَفْض (lowering) · خَافِضَة (that which brings down) · انْخِفَاض (a decline) · خَفَضَ جَنَاحَهُ (to lower one's wing, to be gentle)

This is about the Day of Judgement, the Event that is described as **خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ**, one that brings down and raises up. On that Day, every rank that was held in this world will be reversed. Those who were high because of money, lineage or power will find none of it counts. Those who were looked down on for their faith may be among the highest.
"And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy..."
Even for the person who stands at the greatest height of respect in a family, the parent, the Qur'an asks the child to lower his wing. This is the lowering that raises.
The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, Allah raises some people by this Book and lowers others by it."
Al-Khafid is the One who brings down whomever He wills in justice, so that no one rises above the truth and no pride remains unanswered.

The hadith tells us that the same Book that raises one person lowers another. The Qur'an is the dividing line. Those who accept it, honour it and live by it are raised. Those who treat it as decoration or as an enemy are lowered, however high they stand in the eyes of people.

So the safest protection from being lowered by Al-Khafid is to lower yourself before Him. The one who puts his forehead on the ground in sujud, who lowers his wing to his parents, who lowers his voice before the truth, is the one He raises.
Are you lowering yourself before Allah, or waiting to be lowered by Him?
The Exalter, Who Raises Whom He Wills
to raise up, to lift, and to make high.

**رَفَعَ** is to lift something up: a building, a rank, a name, a voice. The Qur'an uses it for the raising of the heavens, the raising of the Prophets' remembrance, and the raising of believers in degrees. This Name, like Al-Khafid, is always best read in its pair.
An active participle: He is the One who continually raises.
He raises the sincere, the humble, the people of knowledge and of faith, in this world and in the next.
He raised Idris to a high station, raised Muhammad ﷺ's remembrance across the whole earth, and will raise every believer by degrees.
الرَّافِعُ: The One who raises whom He wills in rank, honour and station, including those the world overlooked.
رَفْع (raising) · رَفِيع (high, exalted) · رِفْعَة (elevation) · دَرَجَات (degrees, ranks)
"Allah will raise those who have believed among you and those who were given knowledge, by degrees."
Two groups are named: the believers, and those who were given knowledge. The ayah does not say the rich, or the famous. The raising of Ar-Rafi' is by faith and by knowledge.

Now think about this ayah. Five times a day, in every part of the world, the name of Muhammad ﷺ is called out in the adhan. Raised. The man who was once an orphan in a small town was raised by Ar-Rafi' to a remembrance that no king ever had.
The Prophet Idris. Raised to a high station. Allah raises the people He wishes, in the way He wishes, and sometimes in a way that is hidden from everyone.
The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah does not increase a servant who forgives except in honour, and no one humbles himself for the sake of Allah except that Allah raises him."
Ar-Rafi' is the One who raises whom He wills in rank and station, and who lifts the humble who have lowered themselves for His sake.

Everyone wants to be raised, and the world has a thousand ways of promising it. The hadith tells you the real way, and it is the opposite of what the ego expects: lower yourself for Allah and He will raise you. Forgive, and you are given honour. Give, and you are not made poorer.

Do not mistake the world's lifting for His. A person can be raised in the eyes of people and lowered in the sight of Allah, and a person can be unnoticed on earth and highly raised with Him. What counts is the raising that comes from the Raiser.
Where are you seeking to be raised, in the eyes of people or in the sight of Allah?
The Bestower of Honour
might and honour; the same root as Al-'Aziz (Name 8).

This is the same root as Al-'Aziz, in a form that means *to cause someone to have honour*. Al-'Aziz possesses all 'izzah; Al-Mu'izz is the One who grants it. That is why this Name is read together with Al-Mudhill, in the pair that follows.
This is the form of a verb that causes something to happen to another: أَعَزَّ means to make someone honoured.
So Al-Mu'izz is the One who gives honour to whomever He wills, and who alone has the power to do so.
No one can honour someone whom Allah has not honoured, and no one can take away honour that He has given.
الْمُعِزُّ: The One who bestows honour and strength upon whomever He wills, and no one can lessen what He has honoured.
عِزَّة (honour, might) · عَزِيز (mighty) · أَعَزَّ (to honour) · تَعْزِيز (strengthening)
"...and You honour whom You will..."
This is the same ayah we met in Al-Malik. There the Name was Sovereignty; here it is honour. The one who owns the kingdom owns the honour, and gives it to whoever He chooses.
"Do they seek with them honour? But indeed, honour belongs to Allah entirely."

The people the ayah describes went looking for honour in the wrong place: in alliance with those who would give them status. The answer is blunt and kind at once. Honour is not found there. Go to the One who owns it.
The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah does not increase a servant who forgives except in honour." You would think forgiving costs you your standing. The Prophet ﷺ says the opposite.
Al-Mu'izz is the One who bestows honour and strength on whomever He wills. True honour is only what He gives, and it cannot be taken by anyone else.

Honour that is given by people can be taken by people. A title, a following, an appearance of success can all vanish by next year. The honour that Al-Mu'izz gives stays, because it is not built on anything that can be removed.

The strange secret of this honour is how it is earned. Not by pushing yourself above others, but by forgiving, by being truthful when it costs you, by standing for what is right when it is not popular, by staying humble before Allah. You do not have to defend your dignity when you know who gave it to you.
Where have you been looking for honour that only Allah can give?
The Humbler of the Arrogant
lowness, being brought low; also yielding and softness.

This root is a good example of how one word can carry two opposite shades. **ذُلّ** can mean humiliation, the lowness of someone brought down. It can also mean a willing humility, the lowering of oneself before someone you love and honour. The Qur'an praises believers who are **أَذِلَّةٌ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ**, gentle and humble toward other believers (5:54).
As with Al-Khafid, this Name must be understood together with its pair, Al-Mu'izz. He humbles in justice, and for a reason.
The causative form again: Al-Mudhill is the One who brings someone to lowness.
He humbles whoever raises himself against Him, whoever rejects the truth out of pride, and whoever oppresses His servants.
His humbling is never unjust. It is a response, and it is always the result of what a person chose.
الْمُذِلُّ: The One who humbles whoever He wills, in perfect justice, including those who proudly rejected the truth.
ذُلّ (lowness, humiliation) · ذَلِيل (humbled) · إِذْلَال (humbling) · أَذِلَّة (humble ones)
"...and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is [all] good."
Look at the words that come straight after: **بِيَدِكَ الْخَيْرُ**, "in Your hand is all good." Even the humbling comes from a hand that is only good. There is no randomness or cruelty in it.

This is Iblis. He was not lowered for being created from fire. He was lowered for **تَتَكَبَّرَ**, for arrogance. The first act of humbling in history was a response to pride, which is why the believer treats pride as the most dangerous disease of the heart.
"And he whom Allah humiliates, for him there is no bestower of honour. Indeed, Allah does what He wills."
No one can lift up the one that Allah has lowered, and no one has any complaint against His justice.
Al-Mudhill is the One who humbles whomever He wills in perfect justice, so that no arrogance goes unanswered and no one stands above the truth.

Two kinds of lowness are in front of you. There is the lowness you choose, before Allah, in sujud, in tears, in saying *I was wrong*. And there is the lowness that He brings on someone who refused to choose it. The first leads to honour; the second to ruin.

So take the humility yourself, while it is still a gift. Humble yourself to your Lord. Be gentle with the believers. Be the one who says sorry first. The one who is humble by choice never meets the humbling that is by force.
Is there a place in your life where you must lower yourself before Allah, before someone else lowers you?
The Names That Come in Pairs
Al-Qabid & Al-Basit · Al-Khafid & Ar-Rafi' · Al-Mu'izz & Al-Mudhill
1. Why These Names Come in Pairs

Most of the Names of Allah can be said on their own. These six go in pairs. A single one, heard alone, could give a wrong impression, as if Allah only takes, only lowers, only humbles. The Prophet ﷺ himself said them together: *"Indeed Allah is the One who sets prices, the One who constricts, the One who expands, the Provider"* (Sunan Abi Dawud 3451). And many scholars point out that these Names should be used together, so that the full meaning is clear: He has complete power over both, and He uses each with perfect wisdom.
He gives and withholds · He raises and lowers · He honours and humbles, always in wisdom, never in cruelty, never in randomness.
2. The Three Pairs
Pair
The two sides
Al-Qabid · Al-Basit
Constricts · Expands. Provision, ease, and even the heart itself.
Al-Khafid · Ar-Rafi'
Lowers · Raises. Ranks, stations and the Day of Judgement.
Al-Mu'izz · Al-Mudhill
Honours · Humbles. Who truly holds honour and who loses it.
3. A Test of Reading Correctly

This is perhaps the most important ayah for understanding these pairs. A person is given wealth and says, *my Lord has honoured me.* The same person is constricted and says, *my Lord has humiliated me.* And the very next ayah answers both with one word:

No. Neither expansion nor constriction is the measure of your worth with Allah. Both are tests. The person who is given much is asked how he thanks; the person who is given little is asked how he is patient. The true raising and the true lowering are decided by something else entirely: taqwa. As the Qur'an says, *"the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you"* (49:13).
4. What Each Pair Teaches
Al-Qabid and Al-Basit: your provision and your heart
They teach that wealth and ease are not signs of being loved, and tightness is not a sign of being forsaken. Both are from the same wise hand, and both are meant to bring you back to Him.
Al-Khafid and Ar-Rafi': your rank
They teach that rank, as the world gives it, is not the same as rank with Allah. The one who lowers himself before Him is raised; the one who raises himself above Him is lowered.
Al-Mu'izz and Al-Mudhill: your honour

They teach where honour truly comes from. *"Whoever desires honour, then to Allah belongs all honour"* (35:10). It is never taken by force and it is never given by the crowd. It is given by Him, and withdrawn by Him, in justice.

Allah holds every opposite in His hand: He gives and withholds, raises and lowers, honours and humbles. In all of it He is wise, and in all of it He is Just, so that the believer is steady in ease and in hardship, since both are His and both are His care.

In every season of your life, ask yourself which side of the pair you are standing on, and what Allah is asking of you there. If you are in expansion, the question is *gratitude and generosity*. If you are in constriction, the question is *patience and trust*. If you feel raised, the question is *humility*. If you feel lowered, the question is *return*. In both, He is near.
The All-Hearing
to hear, and also to listen and respond.
The pattern of an established quality: His hearing is part of who He is. It is not something He does only sometimes.

The scholars explain two meanings of this Name. First, He hears everything: every sound, every whisper, every silent thought that the heart says. Second, He hears in order to respond. This is the sense in the words we say in prayer, **سَمِعَ اللَّهُ لِمَنْ حَمِدَهُ**: Allah has heard, and answered, the one who praised Him.

And His hearing is not like ours. The Qur'an gives the rule: *"There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing"* (42:11). We affirm what He has described, and we do not compare it to anything.
السَّمِيعُ: The One who hears every sound and every whisper, near or far, loud or hidden, and who hears the call of His servants and answers.
سَمْع (hearing) · مَسْمُوع (what is heard) · اسْتِمَاع (listening) · اسْتَجَابَ (to answer)

This ayah was revealed about a woman who came to the Prophet ﷺ in distress, speaking about her husband. Aisha said: *"Blessed is He whose hearing encompasses all sounds. I was in the corner of the room and could not hear some of what she said, and Allah revealed: Allah has heard the speech of the one who argues with you..."* (Sunan Ibn Majah 188). A woman's private complaint, spoken quietly, was heard from above the seven heavens and a revelation came down because of it.

Musa and Harun are being sent to Pharaoh, the most powerful man alive. They are afraid. And the answer is two words of presence: **أَسْمَعُ وَأَرَى**, "I hear and I see." That was enough for them to go.
"Our Lord, accept [this] from us. Indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing."

Look at who is saying this. Ibrahim and Ismail, raising the walls of the Ka'bah, a work of the greatest honour, and the last thing they do is ask: please accept it. And they call Him by exactly this Name.

When the companions were raising their voices in dhikr on a journey, the Prophet ﷺ said: "O people, be gentle with yourselves. You are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. You are calling upon One who is All-Hearing and near."
As-Sami' is the One whose hearing encompasses every sound, who hears the whisper of the heart as clearly as the loudest voice, and who answers the call of those who turn to Him.

There are things you could never say to anyone: a fear, a shame, a hope that you are afraid will be laughed at. As-Sami' has heard it already. You do not need to find the right words, or the right place. The Prophet ﷺ said you are not calling someone deaf or far away.

And it is also a Name that guards your tongue. If your words reach Him, then the unkind joke, the backbiting, the lie, is all heard. Hold your words with the same care that you want your du'a to be held.
What have you been carrying in silence that you could say, right now, to the One who hears?
The All-Seeing
sight, and the clear perception of a thing.

From this root we also get **بَصِيرَة**, inner sight: the ability to see what something really is, beyond the surface. When the Qur'an says Allah is Al-Basir, it speaks both of seeing and of the complete understanding of what is seen.
Established quality, again: His seeing is perfect and constant.
He sees everything that is visible and everything that is hidden: the ant on a black rock in a dark night, and the intention in a heart.
As with As-Sami', the Qur'an places the two together: **السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ**. Hearing and seeing complete each other, and nothing escapes either.
الْبَصِيرُ: The One who sees everything, the visible and the hidden, with perfect clarity, and who knows the reality of what He sees.
بَصَر (sight) · بَصِيرَة (insight) · مُبْصِر (one who sees) · أَبْصَار (eyes, sights)

Look at how personal this is. He sees you when you stand to pray at night, and He sees your movements among the worshippers. The ayah is spoken to the Prophet ﷺ, but every servant who stands in prayer is in it. No sujud is unseen.
A short and sharp question to the one who thinks nothing is witnessed: *does he not know that Allah sees?*
"Do they not see the birds above them with wings outspread and [sometimes] folded in? None holds them [aloft] except the Most Merciful. Indeed He is, of all things, Seeing."
Notice that this ayah brings back Name number 1. Al-Basir sees every bird in the sky; Ar-Rahman is the One who holds each one up. Seeing and mercy together.
In the hadith of Jibril, the Prophet ﷺ defined ihsan: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."
Al-Basir is the One who sees everything with perfect clarity, the open and the hidden, the great and the small, and who knows the reality behind what He sees.

The highest level of worship, ihsan, is built on this Name. Not fear alone, but the awareness of being seen with love and care. A person who prays as if he sees Allah does not need anyone to watch him. And a person who knows he is seen does not feel invisible when no one else notices his sacrifice.

Take both comforts from it. The unseen good you do, the patient day, the secret charity, the kindness no one thanked, is seen. And the hidden fault is seen too, which is exactly why the doors to repentance stay open: you are not hiding anything from the One you are returning to.
If you knew that your next hour would be watched by the One who sees, what would you change?
The Final Judge & Arbiter
to prevent, in order to set right; hence to judge and to be wise.

Ibn Faris says that this root is built on one idea: prevention, stopping something from going wrong. A judge **حَاكِم** stops injustice between two people. The bridle on an animal is **حَكَمَة**, because it holds the animal back. And wisdom, **حِكْمَة**, stops a person from doing the foolish thing. They all share one root.
Al-Hakam is the one whose judgement ends the matter. No appeal, no overturning, no second court.

Do not confuse it with **الْحَكِيم**, the All-Wise, a Name that comes later in the list. Al-Hakam is the judge; Al-Hakim is the One whose every action is wise. One tells you He decides; the other tells you He decides well.
His rulings are in His laws, in the events of the world, and on the Day when all will stand before Him.
الْحَكَمُ: The One whose judgement is final, who decides between His servants with perfect justice, and whose ruling no one can change.
حُكْم (a ruling) · حَاكِم (judge) · حِكْمَة (wisdom) · حَكِيم (wise) · تَحْكِيم (appointing a judge)
"Then is it other than Allah I should seek as judge, while it is He who has revealed to you the Book, fully explained?"
The Prophet ﷺ is being asked to find any other judge. The question is a rhetorical one, because everything that a fair judge needs is in the One who revealed the Book: knowledge, justice, and power.
"And be patient until Allah judges. And He is the best of judges."
Patience until He judges. That is a command with a comfort inside it: the case is not closed, and the Judge is not absent.
"Indeed, Allah has judged between the servants."
On the Day when the arrogant and the weak who followed them are talking to each other in the Fire, this is the end of the conversation. The ruling has been given.

A man named Hani was called Abu al-Hakam, because his people would come to him to settle their disputes. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Indeed Allah is Al-Hakam, and to Him belongs the judgement." He asked why he had that name, and when he explained, the Prophet ﷺ said it was good, and changed his name to Abu Shurayh.
Al-Hakam is the One whose judgement is final and perfect, who decides between all His servants, and whose ruling can never be overturned.

Look at what the Prophet ﷺ did in that hadith. Hani was doing something good: settling disputes. And still the Prophet ﷺ gently changed the name, because only Allah is Al-Hakam in the complete sense. The believer learns from this to hold his own judgement lightly. You can give an opinion, and you can settle a dispute, but the last word does not belong to you.

There is also a heavy comfort. The wrong that was done to you and never put right, the person who was never held to account, the injustice no court ever saw: none of it is outside the Judge. And none of what you did, no matter how well hidden, will be outside it either. So live in such a way that you are ready for the ruling.
If the Final Judge gave His ruling on your life today, would you be at ease with it?
The Utterly Just
straightness, balance and setting things level and equal.

The root is about balance: to make two things equal, to set something straight, to give each thing its true weight. It is the opposite of **جَوْر**, crookedness and injustice. The word **عَدْل** can also mean a counterpart: something exactly equal to another.
Like As-Salam, this is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a Name. It does not say that Allah is someone who is just. It says that justice is what He is.
That is why the scholars say that no one can be more just than Him, and that all justice in the world is a faint reflection of His.
He is just in what He commands, in what He decrees, and in how He will reckon: never adding to a person's sin and never withholding the reward of a good deed.
الْعَدْلُ: The One whose justice is perfect and complete, who never wrongs anyone in the slightest, and who gives each its true due.
عَدْل (justice) · عَادِل (one who is just) · عَدَالَة (fairness) · اعْتِدَال (balance, moderation) · جَوْر (injustice)
"Indeed, Allah does not do injustice, even as much as an atom's weight; while if there is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward."

Look at the two halves. The first is about justice: not even an atom. The second goes beyond justice: the good deed is multiplied. His justice is the floor, and His grace is above it. Bad deeds are counted as they are; good deeds are given far more than they are worth.
The scales on the Day of Judgement. A grain of mustard seed is brought forward and weighed. Nothing is too small to be seen and nothing will be lost.
"Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct..."
And this is how He expects His servants to treat each other. The Name is not only to be believed; it is to be lived.
In a hadith qudsi, Allah says: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself, and I have made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another."
He is the One who has every right to do as He wills, and still forbade injustice upon Himself. That is the measure of what it means to be Al-'Adl.
Al-'Adl is the One whose justice is perfect and whose reckoning never wrongs anyone, who gives every right its due and rewards beyond what is deserved.

If the Lord is Al-'Adl, then the believer cannot be unjust. Not in a business deal, not in a family argument, not in how he judges a person who disagrees with him. The Prophet ﷺ also told Mu'adh to beware of the du'a of the oppressed, because there is no veil between it and Allah (Sahih al-Bukhari 1496; Sahih Muslim 19).

And it works the other way as well. When you were wronged, you do not have to fight for every last right with bitterness. The matter is in the hands of the One who forbade injustice upon Himself. Hold to justice in your own actions, and leave the complete reckoning to Him.
Is there someone you have been unfair to, whose right you still owe?
The Subtle, The Gently Kind
fineness and subtlety, and gentle kindness.

This one root carries two meanings that fit together beautifully. The first is **fineness**: something so subtle that it cannot be grasped. The second is **gentleness**: to deal with someone kindly, in a soft and caring way. When both are in the same Name, the meaning is that He knows the finest hidden details of what is good for you, and He brings it to you gently.
The pattern of an established quality: this subtlety and gentleness are always in Him.
Al-Ghazali explains Al-Latif as the One who knows the fine details of what benefits His servants and delivers it to them by the gentlest means.
So you may not even know that you are being treated with lutf. The care often arrives in ways that look, at first, like something else.
اللَّطِيفُ: The One who knows the subtlest details of every matter and brings good to His servants in ways that are gentle and unseen.
لُطْف (gentleness, kindness) · لَطَافَة (subtlety) · لَطِيف (subtle) · أَلْطَافٌ (kindnesses)
"Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills. Indeed, it is He who is the Knowing, the Wise."

This is Yusuf, after the whole story. A well, slavery, a false accusation and a prison, and every step led to a throne and to his family coming back together. When he looks back, he does not say "I worked it out." He says: my Lord is Latif. All of it was a subtle plan that none of us could see from inside.
"Allah is Subtle toward His servants; He gives provision to whom He wills."
**لَطِيفٌ بِعِبَادِهِ**: gentle to His servants. Notice that it is a general statement. It is not about the prophets alone.
"...and He perceives all vision, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware."
And the two Names that always accompany this one: Al-Latif for the subtle gentleness, Al-Khabir for the full awareness. The One who is gentle with you knows exactly what you need.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "How wonderful is the affair of the believer; all of his affair is good, and that is for no one except the believer. If something good befalls him, he is grateful, and that is good for him. If something harmful befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him."
Al-Latif is the One who knows the finest details of every matter and brings good to His servants by gentle and hidden means, often in ways they do not notice.

Look back at your own life, and you will find a few moments where something you hated turned out to be what saved you. A closed door that kept you out of something worse. A delay that put you in the right place. A person who left, and the person who came in their place. You did not see Al-Latif working, and yet He was.

So when the thing in front of you does not make sense, do what Yusuf did in the pit: be patient, because the story is not finished. Trust that the same gentle subtlety is still working. And do the same for others. Be latif with the people who are fragile, speak softly, help without making them feel the weight of it.
Looking back, where has Allah been gentle with you in a way you only noticed later?
The All-Aware
knowledge of the inner reality of things, gained by close acquaintance.

**خِبْرَة** in Arabic is not general knowledge. It is the deep, inner knowledge of an expert who knows the thing from the inside. A person who has **خِبْرَة** knows what is behind the surface. That is the shade of meaning in this Name, and it is why it is paired so often with Al-'Alim and Al-Latif.
An established quality: His awareness of the inner reality is always complete.
Al-'Alim speaks of the breadth of His knowledge: that He knows everything. Al-Khabir speaks of its depth: that He knows what is inside, the reality and the secret.
He knows the intention behind the deed, the reason behind the words, and the hidden state of the heart.
الْخَبِيرُ: The One who is fully aware of the inner reality of everything: what is hidden, what is intended, and what is concealed in hearts.
خَبَر (news, information) · خِبْرَة (expertise) · مُخْتَبَر (a place of testing) · اخْتِبَار (a test)
"Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Aware."

The ayah ends with this Name for a reason. Only Al-Khabir can say who is truly the most righteous, because only He knows the heart. People look at the outside. He looks at what is inside, and that is the only measure.
"And sufficient is He to be, with the sins of His servants, Aware."
A comfort to the one who was wronged, and a warning to the one who wronged. He needs no one to report what was done.
Here the Name appears beside Al-Latif, in an unanswerable question: how could the One who created you not know you?
The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah does not look at your appearances or your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds."
Al-Khabir is the One who is fully aware of the hidden reality of all things: the intentions, the secrets, the unseen conditions of every heart.

This Name can be both frightening and freeing. Frightening, because there is no performance you can put on in front of Al-Khabir; He knows when your prayer is for Him and when it is for those watching. Freeing, because no one can misjudge you before Him. You can be misunderstood by everyone, and still be fully known by the One who matters.

It also takes a weight off your judgement of others. You see someone's behaviour; you do not see their heart. Al-Khabir does. When you are tempted to decide who is better or worse, remember that the decision belongs to the One who is Aware.
If the One who knows your heart read your intentions today, would He find them clean?
The Forbearing, Slow to Punish
composure, patience and a steady, mature mind that does not rush.

**حِلْم** is a rich word. It means to stay calm and unhurried when you have every reason to react, and to have the strength to hold back when you could strike. It is not weakness. It is power that chooses to wait. The same root gives **حُلُم**, which can mean a dream, and the age of maturity, because it is about a mind that has become steady.
An established quality: forbearance is always in Him.
Al-Ghazali explains Al-Halim as the One who sees the disobedience of the disobedient and is not provoked into a hasty punishment. He gives time, because He is not afraid that they will escape.
Do not confuse it with weakness or with neglect. His delay is mercy with a time limit. At a time He knows, it ends.
الْحَلِيمُ: The One who sees every sin and does not hasten to punish, who gives time to return, and whose patience is from power, not weakness.
حِلْم (forbearance) · حَلِيم (forbearing) · أَنَاة (deliberateness) · حُلُم (maturity of mind; a dream)

This ayah is stunning if you read it slowly. If Allah were to take people to account for what they earned, there would not be a single creature left on the earth's surface. We are alive, right now, because of this Name. Every day that a person gets to wake up after a sin is a day of Al-Halim.
"And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing."
Here the Name comes beside Al-Ghafur. Forbearance means that He gives time; forgiveness means that He pardons when we use it.
"Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving."
The ayah comes right after one that tells us that every creature in the heavens and earth glorifies Him, but we do not understand their glorification. And still, He is forbearing with us.
The Prophet ﷺ said to Ashajj of 'Abd al-Qays: "You have two qualities that Allah loves: forbearance and deliberateness."

And in another hadith, he said that no one is more patient than Allah upon hearing something harmful: they claim that He has a child, and still He gives them health and provision (Sahih al-Bukhari 6099; Sahih Muslim 2804).
Al-Halim is the One who sees every disobedience and does not hasten to punish, whose patience comes from perfect power, and who gives His servants time to return.

Two reflections. First, about yourself. The time that you have been given after your sins is not a sign that they did not matter. It is an invitation. Do not use His forbearance as an excuse to delay. Treat each day as a chance that was held out to you by a patient Lord.

Second, about others. He is Al-Halim with people who insult Him. Can you not be a little patient with a family member, a colleague, a child? The Prophet ﷺ taught that the strong one is the one who controls himself in anger. When you hold back a harsh word, you are living a small portion of this Name.
With whom are you being quick to anger, when Allah has been patient with you?
The Magnificent, The Supremely Great
greatness in size, in rank and in majesty; also the bone (عَظْم), the strong frame of the body.
The pattern of an established quality: His greatness is always His, in every sense, and cannot be increased or lessened.
The scholars explain that Al-'Azim means that Allah is greater than anything the mind can encompass. The Qur'an says that people *"do not encompass Him in knowledge"* (20:110).
This is not just a description. It is the feeling the heart should have: that anything we say of Him is small next to what He is.
الْعَظِيمُ: The One whose greatness is complete and beyond all comprehension, before whom everything else is small.
عَظَمَة (greatness) · عَظِيم (great) · تَعْظِيم (honouring, glorifying) · عَظْم (bone)
"His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation tires Him not. And He is the Most High, the Most Great."

This is the end of Ayat al-Kursi, the greatest ayah in the Qur'an. After describing His life, His power, His knowledge and His throne, the ayah ends with two Names: Al-'Aliyy, the Most High, and Al-'Azim, the Most Great. The Kursi alone, which is only His footstool, extends over the heavens and the earth. And keeping all of it does not tire Him.
The command to respond to greatness with tasbih. When you know who He is, the natural reaction is to glorify.

"And they did not appreciate Allah as He should be appreciated, while the earth entirely will be [within] His grip on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand. Exalted is He."
The earth, with all its mountains and oceans, will be in His grip. This is the one that we have been treating as the entire world.
The Prophet ﷺ said: "There are two words that are light on the tongue, heavy on the scale, and beloved to Ar-Rahman: Subhan Allahi wa bihamdihi, Subhan Allahil-'Azim."

Notice the last Name in this hadith: **الرَّحْمَٰن**. The book began with Ar-Rahman, and here is Al-'Azim beside it. The One of unbounded greatness is the One of unbounded mercy. The greatest is also the most merciful.

The du'a that the Prophet ﷺ used to say in times of distress: "There is no god but Allah, the Magnificent, the Forbearing. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the Mighty Throne. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the heavens, Lord of the earth, and Lord of the Noble Throne."
Al-'Azim is the One whose greatness is complete and beyond the grasp of any mind, so that everything else, in comparison, is small.

Every time you bend in ruku', you say **سُبْحَانَ رَبِّيَ الْعَظِيمِ**. Not as a formula, but as a recalibration. Your worries, your plans, even the great fears of your life, all of them are small in front of the One you are bowing to. A person who knows Al-'Azim does not collapse in front of problems, because he has seen what real greatness is.

It also quietly reorders your life. When something is truly great in your eyes, you give it your best. If Allah is the greatest, then He should get the best of your time, your attention and your heart, not the leftover. The more the heart holds His greatness, the lighter everything else becomes.
What is great in your eyes today, and how does it compare to the One who is Al-'Azim?
BEFORE YOU BEGIN
The Beautiful Names
"And to Allah belong the best names, so invoke Him by them."
The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one. Whoever preserves them will enter Paradise."

Scholars explain that to "preserve" the Names (**إِحْصَاء**) is more than counting them. It has levels: to memorise them, to understand their meanings, and to call upon Allah by them, and to let them change how we live. This book is written for the second and the third.
How Each Name Is Studied
**Root Word & Meaning.** The Arabic root, the pattern the Name is built on, and what that tells us. Many Names share a pattern, so you will begin to recognise them.
**Qur'anic Connection.** Where the Name appears in the Qur'an, with the ayah itself, and where it is authentic, the words of the Prophet ﷺ.
**Essence of the Name.** The meaning gathered into a few lines, in English and in Urdu.
**For You, the Servant.** What the Name asks of the person who knows it.

Some Names are explained together in a chapter of their own, because the Qur'an itself places them side by side: Ar-Rahman and Ar-Raheem; Al-Khaliq, Al-Bari' and Al-Musawwir; and the pairs Al-Qabid and Al-Basit, Al-Khafid and Ar-Rafi', Al-Mu'izz and Al-Mudhill.

The Hadith

Grades are given where the collection or a recognised scholar states one. Before sharing the book widely, have each reference checked against the primary collection by a qualified teacher.
The list of 99

The sahih hadith says that Allah has ninety-nine names (Bukhari 2736, Muslim 2677). The specific list that this book follows comes from the narration of Jami' at-Tirmidhi (3507). Many scholars note that the enumeration in that narration is a narrator's addition, not the words of the Prophet ﷺ, and that the Names of Allah are not limited to ninety-nine, as in the du'a recorded in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad: *"I ask You by every name that is Yours, by which You named Yourself, or taught to any of Your creation, or revealed in Your Book, or kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You."* Scholars have also differed over a small number of the Names in this list; that is why Al-Qabid, Al-Basit, Al-Khafid, Ar-Rafi', Al-Mu'izz and Al-Mudhill are always read together as pairs.
The explanations

The meanings of the roots and patterns draw on the classical works of language and tafsir, in particular Ibn Faris (Maqayis al-Lugha), al-Raghib al-Isfahani (al-Mufradat), al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Ghazali (al-Maqsad al-Asna) and Ibn al-Qayyim. They are summaries in simple English, not direct quotations, unless they are placed in quotation marks. The reflections under "For You, the Servant" are the author's own and are offered as reminders, not as rulings.
A note on language

Whenever the Names speak of Allah's hearing, seeing, hand, or anything similar, they are affirmed as Allah has described Himself, in a way that befits His majesty and without comparing Him to His creation: *"There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing"* (Qur'an 42:11). The pictures used in this book (a craftsman, a judge, a helmet) are only to help the heart understand, and Allah's is the highest example (16:60).
